periods.analysis: Overall Resident Satisfaction opened this arc at 4.24 score(1-5), comfortably above the >= 4 target and green. That baseline reflects strong summer engagement: the HarborFest intercept survey team, Library Route 12 pop-ups, and the HView Connect email panel all fed clean response files into the September reporting cycle on time. The best news for Council is that satisfaction is not being carried by one department; Parks, Library, Public Works front counter, and Police community outreach all showed steady positive comments in the verbatim review. Data quality was solid, with duplicate mobile responses removed before closeout, so we can use 4.24 as a dependable benchmark rather than a one-off high-water mark.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the monthly HView Connect sampling cadence and keep the survey close date no later than the fifth business day after quarter-end so departments have time to validate comments. Extend the HarborFest-style intercept model to two fall neighborhood events in North Pier and Bayview Terrace to keep the respondent mix broad. Ask each department to tag one visible service improvement in ClearPoint so the next green result is tied to a named action, not just a score.

periods.analysis: Overall Resident Satisfaction remained green at 4.18 score(1-5), still above the >= 4 target, though it moved down 0.06 from 4.24 in 2024-Q3. The dip is modest and seasonally believable: shorter service windows around holidays, storm-response communications, and heavier permit counter volume showed up in the comment coding. Importantly, the reporting cycle stayed on schedule, and Communications completed the Q4 sentiment crosswalk before the Council packet deadline. This is a good example of a green result that still deserves attention, because a thriving, fast-growing city can lose trust quickly if residents feel small frictions are accumulating.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the quarterly satisfaction dashboard, but add a Q4-specific watch line for holiday closures, storm updates, and permit wait-time comments. Have Communications and Development Services test a single-page “what to expect this week” service bulletin during the December rush, then compare resident comments next quarter. Keep departments looking good by asking them to submit one plain-language explanation for any recurring complaint before the report is finalized.

periods.analysis: Overall Resident Satisfaction rebounded to 4.29 score(1-5), up 0.11 from 4.18 in 2024-Q4 and firmly green against the >= 4 target. The rebound aligns with the January “You Said, We Did” recap, faster 311 closure messaging on service request cohorts SR-25-01 through SR-25-03, and strong attendance at the Civic Center open house. I also like the data story here: the survey file was locked two days before the reporting deadline, and department liaisons had enough time to verify the top comment themes. The quarter suggests residents notice when we close the loop quickly and visibly, especially in a city adding households as fast as Harborview is.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the “You Said, We Did” recap and make it a standing first-month-of-quarter deliverable owned jointly by Communications and the City Manager’s Office. Extend the 311 closure-message language to parks maintenance and code compliance cases, using the same short, resident-friendly template. For the next cycle, preserve the early file-lock date so analysis is complete before Council agenda production begins.

periods.analysis: Overall Resident Satisfaction edged up to 4.31 score(1-5), a 0.02 increase from 4.29 in 2025-Q1 and still green above the >= 4 target. This is a smaller movement than last quarter’s rebound, but it is exactly the kind of steady gain we want to see after process changes become routine. Spring outreach helped: the Permit Ready Saturdays pilot, the Shoreline Clean Team route briefings, and youth sports registration support all created positive service touchpoints. Response coverage also improved in the East Harbor growth area after the mobile kiosk was placed at the Ferry Plaza for three consecutive Thursdays.
periods.recommendations: Sustain Permit Ready Saturdays for the next two high-volume months and publish the actual served-count by Friday after each event. Extend the Ferry Plaza kiosk rotation to the South Marina transit stop so newer apartment households are not underrepresented. Keep the scorecard clean by separating satisfaction comments about city service from comments about private development timelines before department review.

periods.analysis: Overall Resident Satisfaction was 4.3 score(1-5), down 0.01 from 4.31 in 2025-Q2, but clearly green and above the >= 4 target. I read this as essentially stable, not a negative turn, especially given summer crowding, beach traffic, and higher call volume during the July heat advisory. Departments did a good job protecting the resident experience: Parks added weekend restroom checks on Beach Route B, Police expanded the Pier Ambassador shifts, and Public Works posted construction detour maps before the Friday commute window. The one data-quality note is that event-based surveys ran a little hotter than the standing panel, so the weighting review was the right call before publishing.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the summer service playbook, especially Beach Route B checks and Pier Ambassador shifts, because those are visible green-result protectors. Extend pre-weekend detour posting to all active arterial permits, with Transportation confirming links by noon each Thursday. Keep watching the event-survey weighting and document the adjustment method in the ClearPoint notes so Council sees a consistent series.

periods.analysis: Overall Resident Satisfaction came in at 4.27 score(1-5), down 0.03 from 4.3 in 2025-Q3 while remaining green above the >= 4 target. This is the second small quarterly easing, so I am not worried, but I am watching it closely and would rather nudge now than explain later. The comment themes point to normal year-end pressure: utility billing questions, holiday construction moratorium confusion, and longer phone queues during staff leave weeks. Finance and Customer Care helped the narrative by clearing the UB-25 late-fee inquiry batch before closeout, which kept the issue from becoming a broader satisfaction drag. The reporting package stayed disciplined, with department confirmations received before the Council packet cutoff.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the utility-billing call script that Finance used for the UB-25 inquiry batch and add it to the Customer Care knowledge base before the next bill cycle. Extend holiday construction-moratorium messaging to permit applicants, neighborhood associations, and the city homepage banner at least two weeks earlier next year. Set a watch item for phone queue abandonment in Q1, and ask Customer Care to report the weekly trend alongside the satisfaction score.

periods.analysis: Overall Resident Satisfaction returned to 4.31 score(1-5), up 0.04 from 4.27 in 2025-Q4 and green above the >= 4 target. That recovery is encouraging because it followed the Q4 watch items rather than good luck: Customer Care used the updated billing script, Communications refreshed the closure calendar, and Development Services added permit-status text alerts for the DS-26-01 cohort. Resident comments show appreciation for clearer expectations, even when the answer is not immediate. From a scorecard-administration standpoint, this was a strong cycle: measures, commentary, and department owner sign-offs all landed before the draft agenda deadline.
periods.recommendations: Sustain permit-status text alerts and expand them from the DS-26-01 cohort to all residential remodel permits under the standard review track. Keep the Customer Care phone queue watch item for one more quarter, but pair it with first-contact resolution so we reward quality, not just speed. Use the Q1 green result in the Council briefing as a concrete example of how timely reporting plus department follow-through improves resident experience.

periods.analysis: Overall Resident Satisfaction rose again to 4.34 score(1-5), up 0.03 from 4.31 in 2026-Q1 and the strongest result in this eight-quarter run, remaining green above the >= 4 target. The arc matters: after the Q4 2024 dip to 4.18 and the smaller softening in late 2025, Harborview has built back steadily through practical service fixes, not slogans. The Q2 lift appears tied to the expanded permit text alerts, the spring neighborhood mini-grants cohort, and the Bay Loop service request sweep that closed visible issues before summer visitors arrived. Data confidence is high because the panel, kiosk, and event responses were reconciled before analysis, and no late department corrections were needed.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the expanded permit text-alert program and set a quarterly adoption target by permit type so the gain is operationalized. Extend the Bay Loop service request sweep model to West Harbor before peak summer, with Public Works publishing route IDs and completion dates. For Council, frame 4.34 as a green result to protect: keep deadlines tight, keep the respondent mix broad, and keep every department linking one service action to the resident satisfaction trend.

periods.analysis: Satisfaction improved to 3.98 but has not reached 4.00. Survey fielding is complete; its findings still need to be presented to Council.
periods.recommendations: Use the November survey briefing to identify service changes residents can see, and retain the below-target distinction.
